newsitem.title: UK: Clarke rows back on remarks about winning EMU argument.
newsitem.headline: Clarke rows back on remarks about winning EMU argument.

text.p: Britain's finance minister Kenneth Clarke on Thursday appeared to row back from remarks he made suggesting Europhiles like him were winning the debate on a single currency within the ruling Conservative party.

BBC radio played a tape of Clarke's comments at an invitation-only gathering of the Conservative Group for Europe at the party conference in Bournemouth on Wednesday night, in which he referred to "local difficulties" in the party over monetary union.
"We do win the arguments inside the Conservative party and we shall continue to do so," he said on the tape.

"We do so in the national interest, which we put above all, and because we have a clear idea of what a partnership of nation states should be like and how Britain should have just as big a role in shaping that as the French, the Germans or any other continental nation."

However, in television and radio interviews on Thursday morning, the Chancellor of the Exchequer insisted he had merely reiterated government policy and that it was the government which had won the argument on the single currency.

Journalists were trying to stoke up a dead story and Prime Minister John Major and Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind had made government policy clear in remarks at the conference on Wednesday, he said.
"I was reiterating the government's policy," Clarke said. "The government policy has come under challenge and I thought Malcolm and the prime minister plainly answered that challenge yesterday."
"I also said that I was repeating the government policy on economic and monetary union. We won the arguments. The prime minister has won the argument on the policy."
The ruling Conservatives are deeply divided over European monetary union.

The government line is that it will decide at the appropriate time whether Britain should join, but the party's powerful "Euro-sceptic" wing is demanding a commitment now that that a Conservative government would never give up the pound.

Clarke, the leading proponent of European integration in the cabinet, said he was against the idea of a united states of Europe but wanted Britain to play a role in the partnership of nations in Europe.
"I am totally against the whole idea of a united states of Europe," he said.
